questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Ask what is happening to the client right now while the wrap stays on.
questions.hintStrategy: When you witness an error in progress, stop it first; reporting and education follow.
questions.stem: The charge nurse observes a newly hired nurse apply a thick layer of a prescribed corticosteroid ointment to a client's eczema patches on both forearms and then wrap the arms in plastic wrap. The order does not mention a covering. Which action should the charge nurse take first?
options: Complete an incident report before the end of the shift
Notify the provider that the ointment was covered
Stop the nurse and have the plastic wrap removed
Plan an in-service on topical medications for next week
optionRationales: Incorrect. Following reporting policy is appropriate, but paperwork comes after stopping the harm to the client.
Incorrect. The provider may need to know, but the wrap keeps increasing absorption until it is removed; stop the harm first.
Correct. Occlusion without an order increases absorption and the risk of skin thinning; removing it prevents harm now.
Incorrect. Education addresses the knowledge gap, but it is a later step and does nothing for the client now.
questions.rationale: Topical medicines are applied in a thin layer and are not covered with an occlusive (airtight) dressing unless prescribed, because covering increases absorption. A thick layer under plastic wrap delivers more corticosteroid into the skin and body, raising the risk of thin skin, stretch marks, and easy bruising without better results. The charge nurse first stops the practice to protect the client, then coaches the new nurse and follows facility reporting policy. The incident report is tempting because it feels like proper procedure, but client safety comes first.
questions.takeaway: Topical steroids: thin layer, no occlusion unless ordered; stop unsafe practice first, then teach and report.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Think about what makes steroid-thinned skin tear and how to avoid it.
questions.hintStrategy: For “most important” care-plan items, pick the intervention that prevents the most likely injury for this client.
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client has taken prednisone daily for 3 years. During a skin assessment, the nurse finds thin, fragile skin with several bruises on both forearms. Which intervention is most important to include in the plan of care?
options: Pad the side rails and use a lift sheet when repositioning
Apply a fragrance-free moisturizer to the arms twice daily
Measure and document the bruises at the start of each shift
Tape dressings directly onto the forearm skin for protection
optionRationales: Correct. Steroid-thinned skin tears and bruises easily; padding and lift sheets prevent bumps and friction.
Incorrect. Moisturizing supports dry, fragile skin, but it does not prevent the bumps and friction that cause new bruises and tears.
Incorrect. Monitoring the bruises is useful assessment, but it does not prevent further injury.
Incorrect. Covering the skin seems protective, but tape can tear steroid-thinned skin when it is removed.
questions.rationale: Some medicines change the skin itself. Long-term steroids thin the skin, making it bruise and tear easily, especially in older adults. The nurse protects the skin from bumps, friction, and pressure by padding surfaces, using a lift sheet, and handling gently. Tape on the skin seems protective but can tear fragile skin on removal. Moisturizing and tracking bruises are reasonable, but they do not prevent new injury the way padding and gentle handling do.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids thin the skin; prevent bumps, friction, and tape injuries.

questions.hintContent: Look at the list for a product that could add to the effect of another medicine.

rows: Thin layer to affected areas twice daily

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with atopic dermatitis comes to the clinic for a follow-up visit. The client reports new bruises on the arms and bleeding gums when brushing teeth. Refer to the Medication List. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Notify the provider about the bleeding and the primrose oil use
Tell the client to apply the primrose oil to the skin instead
Ask the client to bring all supplements to the next visit
Teach the client to use a soft toothbrush and floss gently
optionRationales: Correct. Evening primrose oil may increase bleeding risk with a blood thinner; new bleeding signs need prompt provider review.
Incorrect. Topical use may lower absorption, but it changes therapy without the provider and leaves the current bleeding unreported.
Incorrect. Reviewing supplements is good practice, but waiting until the next visit delays action on active bleeding signs.
Incorrect. Soft-bristle brushing and gentle flossing are practical bleeding precautions, but they treat a symptom and miss the drug interaction.
questions.rationale: Evening primrose oil is a complementary product that may increase bleeding risk in a client who takes a blood thinner such as apixaban. New bruising and bleeding gums suggest that risk is happening now, so the nurse reports the bleeding and the supplement to the provider. A softer toothbrush is tempting as a practical step, but it treats a symptom while missing the interaction. Complementary products should always be reviewed with the provider.
questions.takeaway: Evening primrose oil plus a blood thinner can increase bleeding; report new bleeding signs right away.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Decide which findings show the vacuum is working and which suggest the client is losing blood.
questions.hintStrategy: For device questions, separate signs that the device is working from signs that the client is being harmed.
questions.stem: A 49-year-old client with a large abdominal wound is receiving negative pressure wound therapy. During rounds, the nurse notes several findings. Which finding requires immediate action?
options: Foam dressing that has collapsed firmly into the wound
Small amount of pale yellow serous fluid in the tubing
Client reports a mild pulling sensation at the site
Bright red blood filling the tubing and canister
optionRationales: Incorrect. Collapsed, firm foam shows the seal is holding and suction is working.
Incorrect. Removing extra serous fluid is the purpose of the therapy.
Incorrect. A mild pulling feeling from suction is expected.
Correct. Fresh bright red blood suggests active bleeding into the device, which can lead to significant blood loss.
questions.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy uses a foam dressing sealed with clear film and connected to a vacuum. Gentle suction pulls out extra fluid, draws the wound edges together, and boosts blood flow. Collapsed foam, serous fluid in the tubing, and a mild pulling feeling show the device is working. Bright red blood filling the tubing and canister signals active bleeding, which needs immediate action and provider notification. The collapsed foam may look alarming to a new nurse, but it is the expected appearance of a working seal.
questions.takeaway: With negative pressure wound therapy, collapsed foam and serous drainage are expected; bright red blood in the canister is an emergency.

Request a wound care nurse consultation
Reinforce teaching about protein-rich foods
Measure the wound weekly and record its size
optionRationales: Incorrect. Case managers coordinate care, but they arrange discharge, supplies, and insurance rather than choosing wound treatments.
Correct. A wound care nurse is a consultant for complex or non-healing wounds and recommends a treatment plan.
Incorrect. Protein supports healing, but nutrition has already been addressed, so this does not change the stalled plan.
Incorrect. Tracking wound size is good assessment, but 5 weeks of no progress already shows the plan needs to change.
questions.rationale: An interprofessional team improves outcomes through better communication and fewer complications. A wound care nurse has special training in complex wounds and is consulted when a wound does not heal. The case manager is tempting because that role coordinates care, but case managers arrange discharge, home care, supplies, and insurance rather than wound treatment. More teaching or more measuring keeps an ineffective plan in place and delays healing.
questions.takeaway: A non-healing or complex wound needs a wound care nurse consult.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client with mild eczema and a known ragweed allergy says, “My friend gave me a chamomile cream. I'd like to try it.” Which information is most important for the nurse to provide?
options: “Chamomile may help soothe your mild eczema itching and redness.”
“Keep using your prescribed cream along with the chamomile cream.”
“Chamomile is related to ragweed, so it may cause an allergic reaction.”
“Stop using the chamomile cream right away if your skin starts to burn.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Chamomile may soothe irritation, but this does not address the client's specific allergy risk.
Incorrect. Using complementary products alongside prescribed care is correct, but it misses the ragweed cross-reaction risk.
Correct. Chamomile is related to ragweed, so this client has a specific allergy risk. This safety warning matters most before the client tries the product.
Incorrect. Stopping if burning develops is sound advice, but it reacts after harm; the client first needs to know the specific allergy risk.
questions.rationale: Chamomile, aloe vera, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation, but the evidence is limited, and natural does not mean safe. Any plant product can cause an allergic reaction, and chamomile is related to ragweed, so this client is at particular risk. The client should tell the provider, use it alongside prescribed care, and stop it if burning, rash, or swelling develops. Those points are all true, but the specific allergy warning is the most important information for this client.
questions.takeaway: Chamomile is related to ragweed; clients with ragweed allergy may react to it.

questions.hintContent: Recall the steps of topical application and find the one that follows putting on gloves.
questions.hintStrategy: For procedure items, name the last completed step in the stem and choose the step that comes right after it.
questions.stem: The nurse has verified the order, identified the client, performed hand hygiene, and put on gloves to apply a corticosteroid cream to a client's psoriasis plaques. Yesterday's cream is still visible on the skin. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Apply a new layer of cream directly over the old cream
Apply a thin layer in the direction of hair growth
Gently clean and dry the skin to remove the old cream
Document the appearance of the plaques in the record
optionRationales: Incorrect. Applying over old cream seems efficient, but it builds up the dose and the risk of skin thinning.
Incorrect. This is the correct application technique, but the old cream must be removed first.
Correct. The skin is cleaned and dried, removing old medicine, before a new thin layer is applied.
Incorrect. Documentation is required, but it is done after the medication is applied, not before.
questions.rationale: Safe topical application follows a sequence: check the order and identify the client, perform hand hygiene and put on gloves, gently clean and dry the skin and remove old medicine, apply a thin layer and rub it in gently in the direction of hair growth, avoid occlusion unless prescribed, then remove gloves, perform hand hygiene, and document. Applying over old cream is tempting because it seems efficient, but it builds up the dose and the risk of skin thinning.
questions.takeaway: Remove old topical medicine and dry the skin before applying a new thin layer.

questions.hintStrategy: When a safety breach is about to happen, choose the option that prevents it rather than one that corrects it later.
questions.stem: A nursing student is about to apply a new dressing to a client's burn wound immediately after debridement. The nurse notices the student is wearing clean, nonsterile gloves and holding a dressing that was opened earlier and left on the bedside table. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Hand the student a pair of sterile gloves to put on
Open a new sterile dressing for the student to use
Stop the student and have sterile supplies and technique used
Discuss the technique with the student after the dressing is on
optionRationales: Incorrect. Sterile gloves are needed, but the dressing that sat open on the table is still contaminated.
Incorrect. A new sterile dressing is needed, but clean gloves would still contaminate it.
Correct. Burned skin has lost its barrier, so dressings are applied with sterile technique. Both the gloves and the dressing must be sterile.
Incorrect. Avoiding embarrassment is considerate, but waiting allows contamination of an open burn wound.
questions.rationale: Burns are treated with daily debridement and sterile dressings. Burned skin has lost its protective barrier, and the dead tissue left behind is a favorite place for bacteria, so dressings are applied with sterile technique. The nurse stops the student before contamination occurs; replacing only the gloves or only the dressing still leaves a break in sterile technique. Discussing it afterward is tempting because it avoids embarrassing the student, but client safety comes before comfort, and the teaching can happen privately once the risk is removed.
questions.takeaway: Burn dressings are sterile; stop a break in technique before it reaches the client.

questions.hintContent: Consider how skin thickness on the face and groin changes how much drug is absorbed.
questions.hintStrategy: When a client reports an unsafe self-care change, stop the unsafe practice first, then involve the provider.
questions.stem: A 31-year-old client was prescribed a high-potency corticosteroid ointment for thick psoriasis plaques on the elbows and knees. At a follow-up visit, the client says, “It works so well that I've also been putting it on my face and in my groin where it itches.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Tell the client to stop using it on the face and groin and inform the provider
Teach the client to use a thinner layer of it on the face and groin
Suggest an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream for the face and groin
Schedule a dermatology visit to have the face and groin skin checked
optionRationales: Correct. Strong steroids are not used on the face or skin folds because thin skin absorbs more and thins easily.
Incorrect. A thin layer is correct technique on the plaques, but high-potency steroids should not be used on the face or skin folds at all.
Incorrect. A milder steroid may suit thin skin, but choosing a new treatment is the provider's decision, not the nurse's.
Incorrect. A follow-up exam is reasonable, but the client would keep applying the strong steroid until the visit.
questions.rationale: High-potency corticosteroids are applied in a thin layer only to the plaques, for the prescribed short course, and not to the face or skin folds, because thin skin absorbs more medicine and thins easily. The nurse instructs the client to stop applying it to those areas and informs the provider, who can assess the itching and the skin there. Using a thinner layer or scheduling a visit seems reasonable, but the harmful use must stop first, and recommending another product is outside the nurse's role.
questions.takeaway: Strong topical steroids do not go on the face or skin folds; thin skin absorbs more.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Identify the client's actual barrier: is it a treatment question or a logistics question?
questions.hintStrategy: Match the client's need to the team member's job, not to the body part involved.
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client will be discharged tomorrow with a large abdominal wound that needs daily dressing changes. The wound care nurse has written a treatment plan, but the client says, “I don't have any supplies at home, and I'm not sure my insurance covers nurse visits.” Which team member should the nurse contact first?
options: The wound care nurse
The case manager
The surgeon
The charge nurse
optionRationales: Incorrect. The wound care nurse designs wound treatment, but the plan is already written; supplies and insurance are not this role.
Correct. Case managers plan discharge, arrange home care, equipment, and supplies, and coordinate insurance.
Incorrect. The surgeon manages the wound medically, but does not arrange supplies, home health, or insurance coverage.
Incorrect. The charge nurse can help with unit issues, but discharge resources and insurance are coordinated by the case manager.
questions.rationale: An interprofessional team works best when each member contributes from their role. The case manager plans discharge, arranges home health, equipment, and supplies, and coordinates insurance, which is exactly what this client needs. The wound care nurse is tempting because the issue involves a wound, but the treatment plan is already done. The nurse teaches the client and family and makes sure everyone shares the same plan.
questions.takeaway: Case manager = discharge planning, home care, supplies, and insurance.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Decide whether the teen's complaints are expected effects or warning signs.
questions.hintStrategy: For “best response” items, choose the option that is accurate and keeps the client on effective therapy when the problem is manageable.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old using benzoyl peroxide gel for 1 week tells the school nurse, “My skin is a little dry and flaky, and the gel bleached my pillowcase. I'm going to quit.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Those are signs of an allergic reaction, so stop the gel and see your provider.”
“It can take several weeks to see results, so try to keep using it.”
“Switch to a gentle cleanser and ask your provider about the dryness.”
“Some dryness is expected. An oil-free moisturizer and white linens can help.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping would be right for burning, blistering, or swelling, but mild dryness and bleaching are expected effects.
Incorrect. This is true and encouraging, but it does not address the dryness or the bleached fabric that are making the teen quit.
Incorrect. A gentle cleanser helps, but this skips reassurance that dryness is expected and ignores the bleaching concern.
Correct. Mild dryness and bleaching are expected effects that can be managed while continuing the medicine. This response addresses both concerns.
questions.rationale: Benzoyl peroxide is the first-line acne treatment because it kills bacteria and unplugs oil ducts. Some dryness, redness, and peeling are expected at first and are eased with a gentle, oil-free moisturizer, and the product bleaches fabric and hair, so white towels and pillowcases help. Improvement takes several weeks. Calling the dryness an allergy is tempting, but mild effects are expected; burning, blistering, or swelling would be reasons to stop.
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide: mild dryness and bleaching are expected; manage them and keep going.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Picture the clog of dead skin in the pore and which product acts like a drain cleaner.
questions.hintStrategy: When two drugs treat the same problem, separate them by mechanism and watch for a mechanism attached to the wrong drug.
questions.stem: A 17-year-old with blackheads and a few red pimples asks how the salicylic acid face wash recommended by the pharmacist works. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “It kills the bacteria that cause acne, which is why it bleaches towels.”
“It calms your hormones so your oil glands make less oil.”
“It shrinks your oil glands so they make much less oil.”
“It loosens dead skin cells so they shed and don't plug your pores.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Killing bacteria and bleaching fabric describe benzoyl peroxide, not salicylic acid.
Incorrect. Hormones do drive oil production in acne, but hormone-based treatments are prescription medicines, not a face wash.
Incorrect. Shrinking oil glands describes oral isotretinoin used for severe acne, not salicylic acid.
Correct. Salicylic acid exfoliates and also reduces inflammation. It loosens dead cells so they shed instead of plugging the pores.
questions.rationale: Acne forms when hormones increase oil (sebum), oil and dead skin cells plug the duct, and bacteria grow in the plug. Salicylic acid works by exfoliation, loosening the glue between dead skin cells so they shed and don't plug pores, and it reduces inflammation. The bacteria-killing explanation is tempting because acne medicines are often grouped together, but that is how benzoyl peroxide works. Like benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid can cause dryness, so it is started slowly.
questions.takeaway: Salicylic acid exfoliates and reduces inflammation; benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs ducts.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Consider how darker skin responds to inflammation and irritation.
questions.hintStrategy: For diversity items, avoid both stereotypes and one-size-fits-all answers; choose care tailored to the documented difference.
questions.stem: A 24-year-old client with dark brown skin has mild acne. The client says, “Even after my pimples heal, dark spots stay for months.” Which plan should the nurse anticipate?
options: An over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide gel used alone
The same plan as any client, since skin tone does not matter
Combination therapy chosen carefully by a skin specialist
Oral antibiotics started now to clear the acne quickly
optionRationales: Incorrect. Benzoyl peroxide is first-line for mild acne, but alone it does not address the lasting dark spots, and it can irritate darker skin.
Incorrect. This sounds fair, but culturally competent care recognizes that darker skin responds differently to inflammation and treatment.
Correct. Darker skin is prone to inflammation and lasting dark spots, so combination therapy may be needed and chosen with care.
Incorrect. Oral antibiotics are used for moderate to severe acne, and they do not address dark spots; this client's acne is mild.
questions.rationale: Darker skin is more prone to inflammation, and after a pimple heals it often keeps a dark spot for months. Clients with darker skin may need combination therapy, such as medicines plus chemical peels or microdermabrasion done by a skin specialist. Because these treatments can also irritate darker skin, they are chosen and done carefully. The one-size-fits-all answer is tempting because it sounds fair, but culturally competent care recognizes real differences in skin response.
questions.takeaway: Darker skin is prone to inflammation and lasting dark spots, so acne plans may combine therapies chosen carefully.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Ask whether the client's past sun experience applies while taking this drug.
questions.hintStrategy: For “needs further teaching,” look for a statement that relies on the client's old habits instead of the new risk.
questions.stem: A 33-year-old client is starting doxycycline for a skin infection and leaves for a beach trip next week. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I rarely burn, so I can skip sunscreen while I'm on this.”
“I'll wear a hat and sit in the shade during midday.”
“I'll use an SPF 30 or higher sunscreen when I'm outdoors.”
“I'll tell my provider right away if I get a bad sunburn.”
optionRationales: Correct. Doxycycline increases sun sensitivity regardless of usual tanning ability, so sun protection is needed.
Incorrect. Shade and protective clothing reduce sun exposure.
Incorrect. SPF 30+ sunscreen is recommended with sun-sensitizing drugs.
Incorrect. A severe reaction should be reported.
questions.rationale: Some medicines taken for other problems change the skin. Doxycycline, an antibiotic, increases sun sensitivity, so clients taking it need shade, protective clothing, and SPF 30 or higher sunscreen outdoors. A client's usual ability to tan does not protect against a drug-induced reaction. The other statements reflect correct teaching.
questions.takeaway: Doxycycline increases sun sensitivity; teach shade, protective clothing, and SPF 30+ sunscreen.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Sort each problem as minor and short-lived or chronic and inflammatory.
questions.hintStrategy: For “which client” items, find the one that differs from the others in the key feature named in the stem.
questions.stem: The clinic nurse is reviewing four calls. Which client should the nurse advise to see the provider for a prescription treatment rather than an over-the-counter (OTC) product?
options: A teen with a few whiteheads on the forehead
An adult with a long-standing, itchy eczema flare
A child whose school sent home a note about head lice
An adult with a mild sunburn after a picnic
optionRationales: Incorrect. Minor acne is usually treated with OTC benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid.
Correct. Eczema is a long-lasting inflammatory condition treated with prescription medicines.
Incorrect. Lice are usually treated with OTC shampoos or lotions.
Incorrect. Mild sunburn is usually managed with OTC soothing products and cool compresses.
questions.rationale: OTC medicines treat minor problems that clients can often manage at home: minor acne, lice, and sunburn. Eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis are longer-lasting inflammatory conditions that need a provider to diagnose and manage, usually with prescription topical or oral medicines. Head lice may seem more serious because they spread, but they are routinely treated with OTC products and careful teaching.
questions.takeaway: OTC: minor acne, lice, sunburn. Prescription: eczema, psoriasis, dermatitis.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.hintContent: Find the response that is both accurate about the evidence and respectful of the client's choice.
questions.hintStrategy: For therapeutic responses, avoid absolute statements and choose the one that is truthful and keeps the client engaged.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with psoriasis says, “I read that aloe vera is natural, so I'm going to use it instead of the steroid cream my dermatologist prescribed.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Aloe may soothe your skin, but use it with your prescribed cream, not instead.”
“Aloe can soothe irritated skin, so it is fine to put it on your plaques.”
“Aloe has not been shown to work for psoriasis, so you should not use it.”
“Let's look at your plaques together first to see how they are doing.”
optionRationales: Correct. Complementary products have limited evidence and should be used alongside prescribed care. This response supports the client's interest and keeps the cream in place.
Incorrect. Aloe may soothe irritation, but this response never addresses the plan to stop the prescribed steroid.
Incorrect. Discouraging substitution is the goal, but the evidence is limited rather than absent, and a dismissive answer may push the client away.
Incorrect. Assessment is useful, but it sidesteps the client's plan to replace effective treatment, which needs to be addressed now.
questions.rationale: Aloe vera, chamomile, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation and promote healing, but the evidence is limited. Complementary products should be used alongside prescribed care, never instead of it, and the provider should know about every product. Saying aloe does not work at all is tempting because it discourages substitution, but it is inaccurate and can push the client away. The best response respects the client's interest while keeping effective treatment in place.
questions.takeaway: Complementary products are used alongside, not instead of, prescribed care, and the provider should know about them.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Think about what suction physically does to fluid and tissue in a sealed wound.
questions.hintStrategy: When options promise that a therapy makes other treatments unnecessary, be cautious; absolutes are usually wrong.
questions.stem: A 60-year-old client with a large leg wound is starting negative pressure wound therapy. The client asks, “How is a vacuum supposed to help my wound heal?” Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: “The suction pulls out the extra fluid, which keeps the wound cleaner and drier.”
“Gentle suction removes extra fluid, pulls the edges together, and boosts blood flow.”
“The vacuum seals the wound tightly under the film so germs cannot get into it.”
“The suction draws out the dead tissue so the wound can heal faster than before.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Removing extra fluid is one effect, but this leaves out pulling the edges together and boosting blood flow.
Correct. These are the three ways negative pressure wound therapy promotes healing.
Incorrect. The clear film does seal the dressing, but that is not how the vacuum promotes healing.
Incorrect. Removing dead tissue is debridement; the device removes fluid and does not replace debridement.
questions.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy is used for severe wounds. A foam dressing is placed in the wound and sealed with clear film, and a tube connects it to a vacuum device. Gentle suction pulls out extra fluid, draws the wound edges together, and increases blood flow to promote healing. The fluid-only explanation is tempting because it is partly true, but it is incomplete, and the device does not replace antibiotics or debridement.
questions.takeaway: Negative pressure wound therapy removes extra fluid, draws edges together, and increases blood flow.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each task needs clinical judgment or is a routine care task.
questions.hintStrategy: For delegation items, prescription medications, teaching, and evaluation stay with the licensed nurse.
questions.stem: The RN is caring for a hospitalized client with psoriasis who has a prescribed corticosteroid ointment twice daily. Which task is appropriate for the RN to delegate to the nursing assistant?
options: Apply the prescribed corticosteroid ointment to the plaques
Evaluate whether the plaques are improving with treatment
Teach the client to avoid applying the ointment to the face or skin folds
Bathe the client with a mild cleanser and report new skin changes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Administering a prescription medication is an RN responsibility in this setting.
Incorrect. Evaluating response to treatment requires RN judgment.
Incorrect. Teaching is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Bathing and reporting observations are within the nursing assistant's role.
questions.rationale: Nursing assistants bathe, turn and reposition, keep skin clean and dry, and report skin changes to the nurse. Administering prescription medications, evaluating treatment response, and teaching require RN knowledge and judgment. Applying the ointment is tempting because it seems like simple skin care, but it is medication administration and needs assessment of the skin and the drug's effects.
questions.takeaway: Nursing assistants bathe and report skin changes; the RN gives medications, teaches, and evaluates.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Identify the client's misconception before choosing what to teach.
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching items, the best response corrects the specific misconception the client voiced.
questions.stem: A 19-year-old client has been using benzoyl peroxide gel four times a day and a salicylic acid scrub twice a day for 1 week. The face is red and peeling, and the client says, “These are store-bought, so they can't really hurt me.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Stop both products for good and see a skin specialist about your acne instead.”
“Add an oil-free moisturizer each night, but keep using both products as you are now.”
“Stop the scrub, but keep using the gel four times a day so it keeps working.”
“Even store-bought products can irritate. Use a thin layer once daily and build up slowly.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Stopping relieves irritation, but these products are first-line; the problem is overuse, not the products themselves.
Incorrect. A moisturizer eases dryness, but the overuse that is causing the irritation continues.
Incorrect. Dropping the scrub helps, but four daily gel applications is still overuse.
Correct. OTC products still need correct use; starting thin and slow reduces irritation. It corrects the overuse and keeps effective treatment.
questions.rationale: Clients often think no prescription means no risk, and they may overuse products. Both benzoyl peroxide and salicylic acid can cause dryness, so they are started slowly with a thin layer, often once a day, and increased as the skin adjusts. Adding a moisturizer or dropping one product helps only partly if overuse continues, and stopping both products abandons effective first-line treatment. Excessive irritation is a sign of overuse that should be corrected.
questions.takeaway: OTC does not mean no risk; start acne products thin and once daily, increase slowly, and avoid scrubbing.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall how long-term steroids change skin structure.
questions.hintStrategy: For “indicates understanding,” choose the statement that applies the teaching to the client's own daily life.
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 58-year-old client who will take prednisone long term about protecting the skin. Which statement by the client indicates understanding?
options: “I'll take hot showers twice a day to keep my skin clean.”
“I'll scrub any bruises firmly so they heal faster.”
“My skin will get thicker and tougher the longer I take this medicine.”
“I'll wear long sleeves when gardening so I don't scrape my arms.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hot, frequent showers dry the skin and add risk.
Incorrect. Scrubbing can tear thinned skin.
Incorrect. Steroids thin the skin rather than thickening it.
Correct. Long-term steroids thin the skin, so protecting it from bumps and scrapes prevents tears and bruising.
questions.rationale: Steroids taken long term can thin the skin, making it bruise and tear easily. Teaching focuses on protection from bumps and clothing friction, gentle skin care, and sun protection. Wearing long sleeves while gardening shows the client understands how to prevent injury. The hot-shower statement may seem hygienic, but it dries the skin and adds risk.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids thin the skin; teach protection from bumps, friction, and harsh skin care.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Think about how lice spread and how eggs survive a single treatment.
questions.hintStrategy: In teaching SATA, reject any option that exceeds label directions or permits sharing of personal items.
questions.stem: The school nurse is teaching the parent of a 7-year-old with head lice about using an over-the-counter lice treatment. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Follow the package directions exactly
Comb out the nits with a fine-tooth comb
Check the hair again after treatment
Wash bedding and hats in hot water
Apply extra product to make sure all lice are killed
Let siblings share the child's comb after it is rinsed
optionRationales: Correct. OTC lice products must be used exactly as labeled to be safe and effective.
Correct. Removing eggs prevents reinfestation.
Correct. Rechecking finds any lice or nits that were missed.
Correct. Hot water kills lice and nits on items the child used.
Incorrect. Using more than directed adds risk without benefit.
Incorrect. Combs and hats should not be shared.
questions.rationale: Head lice are usually treated with OTC shampoos or lotions, but OTC still requires careful teaching. The parent follows the label exactly, combs out nits with a fine-tooth comb, checks the hair again afterward, washes bedding and hats in hot water, and does not let anyone share combs or hats. Using extra product is a common mistake rooted in the belief that OTC means harmless.
questions.takeaway: Lice: follow the label exactly, comb out nits, recheck, hot-wash bedding and hats, and don't share.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Ask of each step whether it controls how much drug the skin absorbs.
questions.hintStrategy: For procedure SATA, include steps from the standard sequence and reject any that change the dose or absorption.
questions.stem: The nurse is applying a prescribed topical corticosteroid cream to a client's eczema patches on the forearms. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Put on gloves before touching the cream
Gently clean and dry the skin, removing old cream
Apply a thin layer and rub it in gently
Rub in the direction of hair growth
Cover the area with plastic wrap to hold the cream in
Apply a thick layer so the cream lasts longer
optionRationales: Correct. Gloves keep the nurse from absorbing the drug and protect the client from germs.
Correct. Clean, dry skin allows good contact and avoids buildup of drug.
Correct. A thin layer is effective and limits absorption.
Correct. Following hair growth reduces irritation of follicles.
Incorrect. Occlusion increases absorption and is used only when prescribed.
Incorrect. More medicine increases absorption and side effects without better results.
questions.rationale: Topical medicine application starts with checking the order, identifying the client, hand hygiene, and gloves. The nurse gently cleans and dries the skin, removing old medicine, then applies a thin layer and rubs it in gently in the direction of hair growth. The area is not covered with an occlusive dressing unless prescribed. Afterward the nurse removes gloves, performs hand hygiene, documents, and watches for irritation or skin thinning.
questions.takeaway: Topical application: gloves, clean and dry, thin layer in direction of hair growth, no occlusion unless ordered.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Weigh each statement against the strength of the evidence and the known risks.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA teaching items, absolute claims such as “cannot” or “cure” are usually the incorrect options.
questions.stem: A 47-year-old client with dermatitis asks about using aloe vera gel, chamomile cream, and evening primrose oil capsules. Which information should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Tell your provider about every product you use
Stop any product that causes burning, rash, or swelling
Use these alongside your prescribed treatment, not instead of it
Products taken by mouth can interact with your medicines
Natural products cannot cause allergic reactions
Strong research shows these products cure dermatitis
optionRationales: Correct. The provider needs a full list to watch for interactions and allergies.
Correct. These are signs of an allergic or irritant reaction.
Correct. Evidence for complementary products is limited.
Correct. Evening primrose oil, for example, may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners.
Incorrect. Any plant product can cause an allergic reaction.
Incorrect. The evidence for these products is limited.
questions.rationale: Aloe vera, chamomile, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation and promote healing, but the evidence is limited. Natural does not mean safe for everyone: any plant product can cause an allergy, and products taken by mouth can interact with medicines. Clients should use them alongside prescribed care, tell the provider about every product, and stop any product that causes burning, rash, or swelling.
questions.takeaway: Complementary products: limited evidence, possible allergies and interactions, use alongside prescribed care, and tell the provider.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.hintContent: Picture the skill set each team member brings, then check each description against it.
questions.hintStrategy: For role-matching SATA, reject options that assign RN-only tasks to assistants or logistics to specialists.
questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing interprofessional roles in skin and wound care with new graduate nurses. Which role descriptions are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: The case manager arranges home care, supplies, and insurance coverage
The wound care nurse consults on complex or non-healing wounds
The oncologist treats advanced skin cancers such as advanced melanoma
The surgeon removes lesions and dead tissue and repairs wounds
The nursing assistant assesses wounds and teaches wound care
The dermatologist arranges home health visits after discharge
optionRationales: Correct. Case managers plan discharge and coordinate home services and insurance.
Correct. Wound care nurses recommend treatment plans for difficult wounds.
Correct. Oncologists manage skin cancers that need more than simple removal.
Correct. Surgeons perform removal, repair, and debridement.
Incorrect. Assessment and teaching belong to the RN.
Incorrect. Arranging home services is the case manager's role.
questions.rationale: An interprofessional team leads to better communication and fewer complications. The nurse assesses, gives medicines, performs wound care, teaches, and coordinates. Nursing assistants bathe, reposition, keep skin clean and dry, and report changes. The wound care nurse consults on complex wounds, the case manager handles discharge logistics, the provider diagnoses and orders, the dermatologist treats skin diseases, the oncologist treats advanced skin cancers, and the surgeon removes lesions and dead tissue.
questions.takeaway: Know each team member's role so the right person gets the right problem.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Recall what the gel does to fabric, to skin moisture, and how quickly it works.
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching SATA, eliminate options that increase skin trauma, such as squeezing, scrubbing, or hot water.
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a 15-year-old who is starting benzoyl peroxide gel for acne. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Start with a thin layer, often once a day
Expect some dryness and peeling at first
Use white towels and pillowcases
Expect improvement to take several weeks
Squeeze pimples gently after applying the gel
Wash your face in hot water to open the pores
optionRationales: Correct. Starting low lets the skin adjust and limits irritation.
Correct. Mild dryness and peeling are expected early effects.
Correct. Benzoyl peroxide can bleach fabric and hair.
Correct. Acne treatment requires patience.
Incorrect. Picking or squeezing pimples worsens inflammation.
Incorrect. Lukewarm water is used; hot water dries and irritates.
questions.rationale: Benzoyl peroxide is the first-line acne treatment because it kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Clients start with a thin layer, often once daily, and increase slowly. Some dryness, redness, and peeling are expected, and a gentle oil-free moisturizer helps. It bleaches fabric and hair, so white linens help. The face is washed gently with lukewarm water, pimples are not picked or squeezed, and improvement takes several weeks.
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide: thin layer, start slowly, expect dryness, use white linens, be patient, never pick or scrub.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Match each row to one of the three goals of the vacuum therapy.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, select only findings that move toward the therapy's goal; a new warning sign is never evidence of success.
questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with a severe sacral wound has received negative pressure wound therapy for 2 weeks. Refer to the Wound Care Notes. Which findings indicate that the therapy is effective? Select all that apply.
options: Wound size
Drainage volume
Wound bed
Odor
Temperature
optionRationales: Correct. The wound has shrunk from 8 × 6 cm to 5 × 4 cm, showing the edges are drawing together.
Correct. Daily canister output decreased from 180 mL to 40 mL as extra fluid is removed.
Correct. More beefy red tissue reflects better blood flow and healing.
Incorrect. A new foul odor suggests infection, not effective therapy.
Incorrect. A temperature rising to 38.3 °C (101 °F) suggests infection.
questions.rationale: Negative pressure wound therapy pulls out extra fluid, draws the wound edges together, and boosts blood flow. Effective therapy therefore shows a smaller wound, less drainage, and a healthier, beefy red wound bed. A new foul odor and a rising temperature are signs of infection that should be reported even when other measures are improving. Evaluating an intervention means comparing results with what the therapy is designed to do.
questions.takeaway: Effective negative pressure therapy: smaller wound, less drainage, healthier red tissue; new odor or fever means infection.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Think about the lost skin barrier and the pain of removing dead tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: For care-plan SATA, select actions that address both the safety risk and the comfort need named in the stem.
questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for a 28-year-old client with extensive burns on the arms who has daily debridement prescribed. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Give prescribed pain medicine timed to work during debridement
Apply dressings using sterile technique
Monitor the wounds for signs of infection
Perform debridement daily as prescribed
Use clean gloves for new dressings to save time
Hold pain medicine until debridement is finished
optionRationales: Correct. Debridement is painful, so pain relief is planned before the procedure.
Correct. Burned skin has lost its barrier, so dressings are sterile.
Correct. Dead tissue in burns supports bacterial growth.
Correct. Daily removal of dead tissue lets healthy tissue grow.
Incorrect. Clean technique is not enough for burn wounds.
Incorrect. Waiting leaves the client in pain during the procedure.
questions.rationale: Burns are treated with daily debridement and sterile dressings. Debridement removes dead tissue that bacteria grow in so healthy tissue can form, and sterile technique is required because the protective skin barrier is gone. Because debridement is painful, the nurse gives ordered pain medicine timed to work during the procedure and monitors for signs of infection. Holding pain medicine until afterward is tempting because the medicine still gets given, but it leaves the procedure unmanaged.
questions.takeaway: Burns: premedicate, debride daily, use sterile dressings, and watch for infection.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.hintContent: Separate the drug's intended effects from signs that the skin itself is being damaged.
questions.hintStrategy: In adverse-effect SATA items, sort each option into therapeutic effect or harm before selecting.
questions.stem: A 57-year-old client has used a prescribed topical corticosteroid on the inner thighs for several months. Which findings at the application site should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: Thin, shiny skin
New stretch marks
Bruises that appear with minor bumps
A skin tear after removing tape
Less redness and scaling than before

questions.rationale: Topical corticosteroids calm redness, itching, and scaling, but long-term or heavy use can thin the skin, cause stretch marks, and make the skin bruise or tear easily. More drug is absorbed where skin is thin, such as the inner thighs and folds. Thin, shiny, easily bruised skin or stretch marks should be reported. Less redness, scaling, and itching are the therapeutic effects the nurse hopes to see.
questions.takeaway: Report thin, shiny skin, stretch marks, easy bruising, or tearing where a topical steroid has been used long term.
